panel.finding_key: packages/notes/src/view/list-empty-bullet-plugin.ts::hand-rolled trim regex backtracks quadratically (redos) on attacker-controlled note content, replacing upstream's linear `.trim()`
panel.summary: Hand-rolled trim regex backtracks quadratically (ReDoS) on attacker-controlled note content, replacing upstream's linear `.trim()`
panel.evidence: `ASCII_TRIM_RE = /^[\x09\x0a\x0b\x0c\x0d\x20]+|[\x09\x0a\x0b\x0c\x0d\x20]+$/g` (lines 19-20) is applied at line 134 to `state.getLines(startLine, nextLine, state.blkIndent, false)` — the full setext-heading paragraph body, i.e. untrusted note text. The first alternative is cheap (`^` without `m` only matches at index 0), but the second, `[ws]+$`, is unanchored at the start: `String.replace` with the `g` flag retries at every offset, and at each offset inside a whitespace run of length k it greedily consumes the rest of the run, fails `$` on the following non-whitespace char, and backtracks one char at a time — O(k) per offset, O(k^2) total. Attack: any workspace member with write access stores content like `x` + `' '.repeat(200000)` + `y\n===` (or the same run on a line above `---`). When a victim opens the note, `NotePreview.render()` (packages/notes/src/view/preview.ts:165) calls `md.render()`, `lheading` matches (level set at line 108) and the trim at line 134 burns ~1e10 backtracking steps, hanging the victim's tab — and re-hanging on every subsequent re-render. Upstream markdown-it's `lheading` trims linearly here, so this quadratic path is introduced by the change. Fix: trim by index scan, or use non-global start-anchored matches, or `String.prototype.trim()`.

🌐 Web query:

`Does markdown-it's Ruler class expose a public way to read a rule's current function by name in versions 14.1.0 through 14.3.0, or is `__rules__` still the only way?`

💡 Result:

In markdown-it versions 14.1.0 through 14.3.0, the Ruler class does not expose a public method to retrieve a rule's function by name [1][2]. Accessing the internal `rules` property remains the standard, albeit unofficial, way to programmatically inspect or retrieve the full list of rules, including their associated functions and states [3][2]. The official public API, such as `getRules(chainName)`, only returns an array of active rule functions without their names or metadata [1][3]. Internal members like `rules` and the `find` helper method continue to be marked as internal and are explicitly noted in the source code as methods that should not be used directly [4][5][6]. Consequently, there have been no changes in versions 14.1.0 through 14.3.0 that provide a supported public API for this purpose [7][8][9].

🌐 Web query:

`markdown-it Ruler source 14.3.0 rules property __rules__ push getRules at`

💡 Result:

In the markdown-it library (version 14.3.0 and other recent versions), the Ruler class manages the sequence of parser rules used during the document transformation process [1][2]. The key components mentioned in your query interact within the Ruler class as follows: rules property The Ruler class maintains an internal array named rules [3][2]. This array stores the configuration for all added rules [3]. Each element in the array is an object containing the rule's name, its enabled state (Boolean), the function to execute (fn), and an array of alternate chain names (alt) [3][4]. push method The Ruler.push(ruleName, fn, options) method adds a new rule to the end of the rule chain [1][5]. When called, it pushes a new object containing the rule details into the rules array and resets the internal cache (setting cache to null) to ensure the next request for rules forces a re-compilation [5][6]. getRules method The Ruler.getRules(chainName) method returns an array of active functions for a specified chain [1][3]. Internally, it checks if the cache (cache) is null; if it is, it calls the compile method to build the rule lookup cache before returning the requested chain's rules [3][7]. Summary of workflow 1. When you use.push, a new entry is added to this.rules [3][5]. 2. The internal state flag this.cache is set to null, invalidating existing caches [3][6]. 3. When.getRules is called, the library runs this.compile if the cache is null [3][7]. 4. The compile function iterates over the enabled rules in this.rules and populates the cache object based on the rule chain associations [3][7].

🌐 Web query:

💡 Result:

In the markdown-it library, the `Ruler` class (located in `lib/ruler.mjs`) is a helper utility used by the core, block, and inline parsers to manage sequences of rules [1][2]. The `this.rules` property is an internal array within a `Ruler` instance that stores the configured rules [1][3]. Each object in this array contains the rule's name, its enabled status, the function (`fn`) to execute, and any alternate chains (`alt`) the rule belongs to [1][4]. Regarding your mention of `tables.mjs`, it refers to one of the specific block-level parsing rules (typically found in `lib/rules_block/table.mjs`) [5]. While `tables.mjs` implements the logic for parsing Markdown tables, it is managed by the `md.block.ruler` instance [6][2]. Key points about the `Ruler` system: 1. Rule Management: The `Ruler` provides public methods like `push()`, `before()`, `after()`, and `at()` to modify the parsing pipeline without editing core library files [4][2]. 2. Internal State: While `this.rules` is exposed on the `Ruler` instance, it is intended for internal use [1]. Direct modification of `this.rules` is generally discouraged; instead, developers should use the provided API methods (e.g., `md.block.ruler.at(...)` to replace a rule) [7][2]. 3. Compilation: The `Ruler` class maintains a `this.cache` property [1]. When `getRules(chainName)` is called, the ruler checks if the cache is null and, if so, compiles the rules into optimized chains for high-speed execution [1][3]. If you are looking to interact with existing rules—such as wrapping a rule or modifying the table parsing logic—the recommended approach is to access the ruler via `md.block.ruler`, use `find` to locate the rule, or use the official API methods to replace or wrap the functionality [7][2].
